data.title: Genital ulcer disease — viva
data.summary: Sexually transmitted infections · 19 viva questions with answers
data.body:
_Viva questions for the case: **Genital ulcer disease** (Sexually transmitted infections)_

**Q1. Give the causes of genital ulcers — infective and non-infective (PYQ: differential diagnosis of genital ulcers).**
- STI: herpes genitalis (commonest in India now), primary syphilis, chancroid, donovanosis (granuloma inguinale), LGV
- Other infective: candidal balanitis erosions, scabies, secondary bacterial infection, tuberculosis, amoebiasis, CMV/HIV ulcers
- Non-infective: trauma (zipper, bites, sexual), fixed drug eruption, Behçet's/aphthae, erosive lichen planus, pemphigus vulgaris, SJS, lichen sclerosus erosions, Crohn's disease, pyoderma gangrenosum, Lipschütz ulcer (acute vulvar ulcer, EBV), SCC, Zoon's balanitis, dermatitis artefacta

**Q2. How do you approach a patient with genital ulcer?**
- History: incubation, number, pain, recurrence, bubo, sexual exposure/partners, drug intake (FDE), systemic symptoms (Behçet's)
- Examination: number, size, edge, base, induration, bleeding on touch, regional lymph nodes (character, uni/bilateral), other mucocutaneous signs
- Investigations: dark-field microscopy, Tzanck/PCR for HSV, Gram stain, Giemsa crush smear (Donovan bodies), serology (VDRL/RPR, TPHA), HIV, biopsy for chronic or atypical
- Treat syndromically if lab not available (NACO kits) and review

**Q3. Compare the main ulcers in a table-like way.**
- Syphilis: painless, single, indurated, clean base, rubbery bilateral nodes, incubation ~3 weeks
- Herpes: painful, multiple grouped vesicles/small erosions, recurrent, tender bilateral nodes, incubation 2–7 days
- Chancroid: painful, multiple, soft, ragged undermined, dirty base, suppurative unilateral bubo, 3–7 days
- Donovanosis: painless, beefy-red, friable, bleeds on touch, extends by continuity, pseudobubo (subcutaneous granulation, no true node), 8–80 days
- LGV: small transient painless ulcer often missed; later painful bubo with groove sign, 3–30 days

**Q4. What is donovanosis? (PYQ: granuloma inguinale)**
- Chronic progressive ulcerative STI by Klebsiella granulomatis (Calymmatobacterium); endemic in Papua New Guinea, South Africa, India (rare now)
- Types: ulcerogranulomatous (commonest, beefy red), hypertrophic/verrucous, necrotic, sclerotic/cicatricial
- Complications: pseudoelephantiasis, stenosis, SCC, haematogenous spread to bone/liver
- Treatment: azithromycin 1 g weekly (or 500 mg daily) for at least 3 weeks until healed; doxycycline 100 mg BD alternative

**Q5. What are Donovan bodies? (PYQ)**
- Intracytoplasmic bipolar-staining ('safety-pin') encapsulated rod-shaped organisms inside large mononuclear cells (macrophages), seen on Giemsa/Leishman-stained crush/tissue smear from ulcer edge — diagnostic of donovanosis

**Q6. How do you do dark-field microscopy?**
- Clean ulcer with saline, squeeze/abrade to get serous exudate (avoid blood), place on slide with coverslip, examine within 20 min under dark-field condenser
- T. pallidum: thin, tightly coiled, corkscrew motility with flexion at the middle (angulation)
- Not for oral lesions (commensal treponemes); negative after topical/systemic antibiotics — repeat thrice

**Q7. Serological tests for syphilis — classify.**
- Non-treponemal (cardiolipin): VDRL, RPR — quantitative, used for activity and treatment response (4-fold fall); false positives (biological false positive — pregnancy, SLE, APLA, leprosy, malaria, IV drug use); prozone phenomenon
- Treponemal: TPHA/TPPA, FTA-ABS, EIA/CLIA, rapid immunochromatographic tests — remain positive for life
- Reverse algorithm (treponemal first, then non-treponemal) used in many labs

**Q8. Treatment of early syphilis.**
- Benzathine penicillin G 2.4 MU IM single dose (after test dose as per local protocol)
- Penicillin allergy (non-pregnant): doxycycline 100 mg BD 14 days (azithromycin 2 g single dose — resistance reported)
- Pregnancy: penicillin only (desensitise if allergic)
- Watch for Jarisch–Herxheimer reaction (fever, myalgia within 24 h); follow VDRL at 3, 6, 12 months

**Q9. What is syndromic management? Advantages and limitations (PYQ).**
- Treatment based on a clinical syndrome (discharge, ulcer, bubo, lower abdominal pain, scrotal swelling, neonatal conjunctivitis) using flowcharts to cover the common organisms at the first visit
- Advantages: simple, quick, treats at first visit without lab, cost-effective, high cure, wide coverage, partner treatment
- Limitations: overtreatment and overdiagnosis, misses asymptomatic infections, poor for cervical infection in women, encourages resistance, no second-line pathway, no aetiological data

**Q10. Name the NACO colour-coded kits.**
- Kit 1 Grey — urethral/anorectal discharge, cervicitis: azithromycin 1 g + cefixime 400 mg stat
- Kit 2 Green — vaginal discharge: secnidazole 2 g + fluconazole 150 mg stat
- Kit 3 White — non-herpetic genital ulcer: benzathine penicillin 2.4 MU IM + azithromycin 1 g
- Kit 4 Blue — non-herpetic ulcer, penicillin allergy: doxycycline 100 mg BD × 15 days + azithromycin 1 g
- Kit 5 Red — herpetic ulcer: acyclovir 400 mg TDS × 7 days
- Kit 6 Yellow — lower abdominal pain: cefixime 400 mg stat + metronidazole 400 mg BD × 14 days + doxycycline 100 mg BD × 14 days
- Kit 7 Black — inguinal bubo: doxycycline 100 mg BD × 21 days + azithromycin 1 g stat

**Q11. What are the '4 Cs' and '5 Cs' of STI management?**
- Compliance, Counselling, Condoms, Contact (partner) tracing — plus Case detection/confidentiality as the 5th
- Also offer HIV and syphilis testing (and hepatitis B)

**Q12. Why is genital ulcer disease important for HIV?**
- Breach of mucosa and recruitment of CD4 cells increase HIV acquisition 2–5 fold and increase shedding; treating GUD is part of HIV prevention

**Q13. Describe the primary chancre in detail.**
- After incubation 9–90 days (average 21): single painless indurated ('button-like') ulcer with clean red base, serous exudate, regular raised border; bilateral painless rubbery non-suppurating inguinal nodes ('satellite bubo'); heals in 3–6 weeks without treatment
- Extragenital chancres: lips, tongue, tonsils, fingers, nipples, anus (may be painful)

**Q14. Describe secondary syphilis skin features.**
- 6–12 weeks after chancre: non-itchy symmetrical macular (roseola)/ papular/ papulosquamous eruption including palms and soles (copper-coloured, collarette — 'Biett's collarette'), condylomata lata (moist flat papules in anogenital area — highly infectious), mucous patches/ snail-track ulcers, split papules at angles of mouth, moth-eaten alopecia, annular lesions on face (dark skin), lues maligna (ulceronodular in HIV); generalised lymphadenopathy, malaise

**Q15. Tertiary and congenital syphilis — skin features.**
- Tertiary: gummas (punched-out ulcers with wash-leather slough, heal with tissue-paper scars), nodular/ noduloulcerative syphilides (arciform), cardiovascular (aortitis), neurosyphilis
- Congenital early: snuffles, vesiculobullous palms/soles (syphilitic pemphigus), condylomata, hepatosplenomegaly, pseudoparalysis (Parrot); late: Hutchinson's teeth, interstitial keratitis, 8th nerve deafness (Hutchinson's triad), saddle nose, rhagades, sabre tibia, frontal bossing, Clutton's joints

**Q16. Interpretation of serology results (VDRL/TPHA combinations).**
- VDRL+ TPHA+: current or recently treated syphilis (use VDRL titre)
- VDRL− TPHA+: treated past syphilis, very early primary (VDRL not yet positive), late latent/ tertiary
- VDRL+ TPHA−: biological false positive (repeat; check APLA, SLE, pregnancy)
- Both negative: no syphilis or incubation/ very early primary (repeat at 2–4 weeks); prozone in secondary — dilute serum

**Q17. What is the Jarisch–Herxheimer reaction?**
- Acute febrile reaction within 2–24 h of first antibiotic dose (penicillin) for spirochaetal infection — fever, chills, myalgia, headache, worsening rash, hypotension — due to release of treponemal lipoproteins/ cytokines; common in secondary syphilis; treat with antipyretics, reassurance; in pregnancy may cause preterm labour/ fetal distress (monitor); not an allergy — continue treatment

**Q18. Treatment of late latent syphilis and neurosyphilis.**
- Late latent/ unknown duration/ tertiary (non-neuro): benzathine penicillin 2.4 MU IM weekly × 3 doses
- Neurosyphilis/ ocular/ otic: aqueous crystalline penicillin G 18–24 MU/day IV (3–4 MU every 4 h) for 10–14 days; procaine penicillin + probenecid alternative; CSF follow-up

**Q19. Syphilis in pregnancy — screening and treatment.**
- Universal antenatal screening (VDRL/ RPR or rapid test) at first visit (and third trimester in high-risk); treat with benzathine penicillin as per stage — only penicillin prevents congenital syphilis (desensitise if allergic); treat partner; evaluate newborn (titres, exam); India's goal — elimination of mother-to-child transmission (EMTCT) of HIV and syphilis

## Quick spotter facts
- Painless indurated clean ulcer — syphilis
- Beefy red friable ulcer, pseudobubo — donovanosis (safety-pin Donovan bodies)
- White kit = non-herpetic GUD

_Sources: Previous-year PG question papers (Sahana P Raju, Solved Papers Dermatology); IADVL Textbook of Dermatology 5e (Approach to genital ulcer); NACO National Technical Guidelines on RTI/STI (syndromic management, colour-coded kits). Answers written in our own words; check with your teachers' preferences._
